1:
The chapter opens on a peace suddenly broken, and the witnesses set the invasion at once in its chronology and its moral frame. The reformed John Gill notes that it came "after this" — after Jehoshaphat's return from Ramoth-gilead and his ordering of the civil and religious affairs of his people, at the very moment he might have looked for quiet and prosperity. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the date more narrowly: the postea throws the war into the latter part of the reign, some six or seven years before the king's death and shortly after the events of 2 Chronicles 18 and 19. They wrestle too with the obscure notice that with the Moabites and Ammonites there marched a third company "from the Ammonites," a partitive phrase they find hard to reconcile with the mention of Mount Seir in v.10 and v.22.

Here the text-critical witnesses divide over who that third contingent was. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke rejects the received "other beside the Ammonites" as a false insertion and, following the Targum, reads "some of the Edomites," since the later verses draw the enemy from Mount Seir. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott prefers, by the transposition of a single Hebrew letter, "the Maonites" — the Meunim of 1 Chronicles 4:41, a tribe seated at Maon on the eastern slopes of Mount Seir, whom Josephus calls a multitude of Arabs and who are named again with Arabs in 2 Chronicles 26:7. So the debate is real: was the ally an Edomite people or the distinct Maonite tribe of the Seir country?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the verse from geography to providence. We left Jehoshaphat, he says, well employed in reforming his kingdom, and expected to hear only of peace; but here he is in distress — "if we meet with trouble in the way of duty, we may believe it is that God may have an opportunity of showing us so much the more of his marvellous loving-kindness." The confederates came from beyond the Dead Sea, marching through the trans-Jordan tribes who gave them passage; chiefly they were the children of Lot, whom the rest helped, as the psalmist rehearses in Psalms 83:6-8. The neighbouring nations had once feared Jehoshaphat, Henry recalls from 2 Chronicles 17:10, but his affinity with Ahab had lessened him in their esteem, and they fancied his God was displeased with him. The witnesses thus knit the verse together: a settled reign, a sudden league of kindred foes, and a distress permitted so that a greater deliverance might follow.
2:
Word of the invasion reaches the king, and the witnesses attend both to the messengers and to a knot in the geography. The reformed John Gill takes the reporters for deserters, spies, or inhabitants of the border districts who rode in haste to warn Jehoshaphat. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the subject is left indefinite — messengers or fugitives, to be supplied from the sense — and that the multitude is said to come "from beyond the (Dead) sea."

The crux lies in the next phrase, "on this side Syria." Keil and Delitzsch judge that me-Aram, "from Syria," yields no suitable sense, since the whole narrative says nothing of enemies out of Syria, and they read with Calmet me-Edom, "from Edom" — for the attack came round the south end of the Dead Sea, from the Edomite quarter. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke argues the same emendation on the narrowest of grounds: the change from Aram to Edom requires no more than the almost imperceptible difference between resh and daleth, and "we do not read of any Syrians in this invasion, but we know there were Edomites." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott concurs that Edom is probably the true reading, a name often confused with Aram, since the invaders marched round the southern end of the sea.

Against this stands the other wesleyan-arminian witness. John Wesley keeps the received "Syria," but reads it largely: Syria so called includes the Moabites and Ammonites, and the word may be chosen on purpose "to intimate that they came by the instigation of the Syrians, to revenge themselves of Jehoshaphat for joining with Ahab against them" at Ramoth-gilead. So the debate is genuine — whether to mend the text to Edom, matching the march and the later mention of Mount Seir, or to retain Syria and find in it a hint of the political grudge behind the war.

On the last name the witnesses are one. Hazazon-tamar, the text explains, is Engedi; the Targum renders it "the wood of palm trees," and Clarke thinks the confederates lay hid there. Gill, Ellicott, and Keil and Delitzsch place it at the modern Ain Jidy, midway along the western coast of the Dead Sea — thirty-six miles, or about fifteen hours, from Jerusalem, the same spot named in 1 Samuel 23:29 and Genesis 14:7. Ellicott notes that the Syriac and Arabic put Jericho for Hazazon-tamar, since Jericho too was called a city of palms. The messengers' report, then, sets the enemy already deep within the land, at the oasis by the sea, and drives the king to the resolve the next verse records.
3:
"And Jehoshaphat feared, and set himself to seek the LORD" — and the witnesses probe first the fear and then the resolve it produced. The reformed John Gill is careful about the cause of the fear. It was not simply the number of the enemy, for the king had forces enough to take the field against them; it was chiefly that the Lord had lately told him, by the seer Jehu, that wrath was upon him from before the LORD, as 2 Chronicles 19:2 had warned, so that Jehoshaphat feared this might be the very time appointed for that wrath to be executed. A guilty conscience, on this reading, sharpened the alarm the invasion brought.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott fasten on the idiom "set himself." The Hebrew, they say, is to "give" or "put" the face toward a thing — the phrase of Daniel 9:3 and 2 Kings 12:18 — and it implies a fixed purpose, a settled determination to seek help of the Lord. Ellicott adds that the construction "to seek the LORD" is that of 2 Chronicles 15:13, and that the proclaimed fast is an act of national self-humiliation, an admission of guilt meant to evoke the divine pity and succour, of a piece with the fasts of Judges 20:26, 1 Samuel 7:6, Joel 2:12-17, and Ezra 8:21.

Keil and Delitzsch draw out the pattern of the response. The report filled the king with fear, and he resolved to seek the Lord; he proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah, that the people might bow themselves before God and beg His help, as was the custom in great misfortunes; and in consequence the whole nation gathered — not the men of Jerusalem only, but out of all the cities of the kingdom they came to seek Him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same movement as a lesson in proportion: Jehoshaphat found he could not possibly stand against so numerous an army, and could expect deliverance only from the strong arm of God; and "to get such extraordinary help, they should seek it in an extraordinary way," hence the universal fast and the gathering of all the people to Jerusalem. The witnesses converge on a single portrait — a king whose fear, whether of the enemy or of the wrath he had been warned of, drives him not to muster alone but to the sanctuary, turning a military crisis into a national act of penitence and prayer.
4:
The nation answers the royal summons, and the witnesses mark how a whole people, not a capital only, converges upon the temple. The reformed John Gill observes that they met "not in their several cities, but at Jerusalem," as the sequel shows — the crisis drew them to one place, the house of God, rather than to scattered local prayers. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the verb: "to ask" is to seek — baqqesh, the synonym of darash used in the previous verse — and the object, rightly supplied by the Authorised Version, is help; the emphatic clause "even out of all the cities of Judah" underlines that the gathering in the temple represented the whole nation, and not merely the men of Jerusalem.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, read the verse as the hinge between the proclamation and the prayer. When the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem had assembled themselves in the house of God, the king came forth before the new court and made his supplication; the seeking "of the LORD" is the seeking of His help by fasting and prayer in the sanctuary, and the people came for it out of every city of the kingdom. The stress falls on the completeness of the response: the fast Jehoshaphat proclaimed did not remain a paper decree but drew the realm together into one supplicating body.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the posture of that body. The people readily assembled out of all the cities of Judah in the court of the temple to join in prayer, and they stood before the Lord, he says, "as beggars at his door" — a nation come to plead, empty-handed, at the threshold of its God. And Henry finds in the chosen place a warrant for their hope: they met in the house of the LORD, before the court lately added to it, and so came within reach of that gracious promise God had made in answer to Solomon's dedication, "Mine ears shall be attentive unto the prayer that is made in this place," recorded at 2 Chronicles 7:15. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the fact that all Judah, from every town, came up to the one sanctuary; Keil and Delitzsch set the assembly as the frame of the king's prayer; Henry reads in the gathering the humility of beggars and the confidence of men who prayed where God had promised to hear. A kingdom under threat has become a congregation at prayer, and the stage is set for the great supplication that follows.
5:
The verse sets the scene of the great prayer — the king standing in the assembly, in the house of the LORD, before the new court — and the witnesses gather around both his place and his posture. The reformed John Gill pictures Jehoshaphat in the temple, in the court of the people where the men of Judah and Jerusalem were gathered, standing "very probably on the brasen scaffold erected by Solomon." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the words the same way: "the house" is largely so called, meaning the court of the people, and the king stood upon that brazen scaffold Solomon had made, taking his place before the priests' court.

On the puzzling name "the new court" the witnesses offer complementary guesses. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the title occurs only here, and probably designates the "great" or outer court of 2 Chronicles 4:9, in which the people assembled; Jehoshaphat stood facing them, in front of the entrance to the Court of the Priests, and the court may have been called new "as having been recently repaired or enlarged," while the Syriac and Arabic read instead "before the new gate." Keil and Delitzsch agree that it is the outer court Solomon built, here named new because it had been restored or extended under Jehoshaphat or Asa; the king set himself before it, at the entrance into the court of the priests, so that the congregation stood opposite him. Wesley adds his own surmise — that it was called new "because it had lately been renewed when the altar was renewed."

Ellicott marks too the pairing "Judah and Jerusalem," recurring at v.27, where the capital is named beside the country as by far its most important part. The witnesses do not divide; they simply reconstruct the tableau. A king stands raised on a bronze platform, as Solomon had stood to dedicate the house in 2 Chronicles 6:12-13, with the whole praying nation ranged before him in the temple court. It is a deliberate echo: the son of David takes the very posture of the temple's founder, and in the place where God had promised to hear, he prepares to spread the kingdom's peril before the God of the fathers. The detail is not idle antiquarianism but the frame the Chronicler builds for the prayer — the representative of the people, in the appointed place, about to plead the covenant on their behalf.
6:
The prayer opens, and the witnesses hear in its first words a deliberate ascent from the covenant God of the fathers to the universal Ruler of the nations. The reformed John Gill glosses "O LORD God of our fathers" of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whose covenant God He was — the appeal grounded from the outset in the ancient bond. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the two great questions that follow. "Art not thou God in heaven?" declares, as in Psalms 115:2-3, that Jehovah, the worship of Israel, is no limited local or tribal deity but God over all; and "rulest not thou over all the kingdoms of the heathen?" echoes David's own prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:12, "thou reignest over all; and in thine hand is power and might." Both clauses, Ellicott insists, should be rendered affirmatively, as statements of faith; and the closing words, "so that none is able to withstand thee," are literally "there is none against thee to stand up," the construction of Psalms 94:16 and of Asa's like petition at 2 Chronicles 14:11.

Keil and Delitzsch lay out the architecture of the whole prayer that this verse begins. Jehoshaphat addresses Jahve, the God of the fathers, as the almighty Ruler over all kingdoms, and then sets forth the circumstances of his case: God had given the land to Israel for an everlasting possession, and Israel had built a sanctuary to His name; yet the people had in no way provoked the Ammonites, Moabites, and Edomites, who now came to drive them out. On these two facts the king founds his plea in a twofold way — recalling the divine promise to hear prayer offered in the temple, and laying weight on Israel's own helplessness against so vast a host.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke stands back to admire the man at prayer. "What an instructive sight was this!" he exclaims — the king who proclaimed the fast was foremost to observe it, and was on this occasion "the priest of the people," offering in the congregation, without form or premeditation, "one of the most sensible, pious, correct, and as to its composition one of the most elegant prayers ever offered under the Old Testament dispensation." The witnesses do not divide. Gill anchors the address in the covenant, Ellicott secures the affirmative force of its rhetorical questions, Keil and Delitzsch trace its logic from creation-wide sovereignty down to Israel's peculiar need, and Clarke marvels at a monarch who leads his people not in arms but in worship — spreading before the God who rules all kingdoms the one kingdom that is helpless without Him.
7:
The prayer now grounds its plea in history and title — the God who drove out the Canaanites and gave the land to Abraham's seed for ever. The reformed John Gill hears in "art not thou our God" a claim of peculiar relation: not merely the Creator and Governor of men, but Israel's covenant God and Father, to whom alone they may turn. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the clause as an appeal to accomplished fact — "didst not Thou, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before thy people Israel?" — the language of Joshua 23:9 and Deuteronomy 4:38; and he traces the gift of the land to the promise of Genesis 13:15-16 and Genesis 15:18, with "for ever" answering the "everlasting possession" of Genesis 17:8.

The title "thy friend" draws the witnesses' warmest attention. Ellicott notes that it is literally "thy lover," the same honour given Abraham in Isaiah 41:8 and repeated by St. James in James 2:23; and he adds the striking after-life of the phrase, that Hebron, the patriarch's burial-place, is to this day known to the Muslim world as el-Khalil, "the Friend." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the word covenantally: God had "engaged himself by covenant to be his friend, and the friend of his seed for ever" — so that Jehoshaphat is not flattering Abraham but pleading a bond God had freely made.

Keil and Delitzsch set the verse within the structure of the whole petition. Israel dwelt in the land God gave and built Him a sanctuary for His name, as at 2 Chronicles 6:5; and by recalling this the king lays the first of his two foundations — the divine promise to answer prayer offered in the temple, a promise sealed when the glory filled the house at 2 Chronicles 7:1-3. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the covenant relation, Ellicott and Wesley the covenant friendship of Abraham, Keil and Delitzsch the covenant gift of the land — and together they show the logic of the plea. Jehoshaphat argues from what God has already done and freely bound Himself to be: if this is the land Thou gavest to the friend Thou lovedst, and this the people of his seed, then the invaders who come to seize it are not merely Judah's enemies but intruders upon Thine own gift, and the honour of maintaining the grant is Thine.
8:
The plea presses on from the gift of the land to the house built upon it — "they dwelt therein, and have built thee a sanctuary therein for thy name." The reformed John Gill reads the dwelling as a long tenure: Israel had lived in the land "from ages past, hitherto, since it was first given them," and had been settled in possession of it — a continuity that itself becomes part of the argument, for the people now threatened with expulsion are the ancient occupants of a divine grant.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott concentrates on the phrase "a sanctuary for thy name," which he treats as a single expression, the counterpart of Solomon's petition in 2 Chronicles 6:5-8 "that my name might be there." The name of Jehovah, he explains, designates all that He is to Israel — His revealed character, His whole self as made known to His people; so that a house built "for His name" is a house bound up with God's own honour, not a mere shrine but the seat of His self-disclosure. Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, add that the clause looks back to the day of consecration, when Israel, in building the house, had voiced the confident hope spelled out in the verse that follows: that whenever evil came, they might stand before this house and be heard.

The witnesses do not divide, and the brevity of the notice belies its weight in the prayer. By naming the sanctuary, Jehoshaphat quietly reminds God of a bargain of His own making. The temple was reared for God's name; its dedication had drawn down the glory that filled the house; and Solomon's dedicatory prayer had asked, and God had granted, that supplication offered toward this place should be heard. To recall the sanctuary, then, is not to boast of Israel's piety — for the house too was God's gift — but to lay hold of the promise attached to it. The people who built the house for the name now shelter under the name in their extremity. Gill fixes the long dwelling that gives Israel its title; Ellicott unfolds what it means that the house bears God's name; Keil and Delitzsch tie the clause to the confident hope of its consecration. Between them they show the second pillar of the prayer rising: first the land God gave, and now the house God claimed as His own, both pledged against the day of trouble that has now arrived.
9:
Jehoshaphat now rehearses the very promise on which he stakes everything — that if evil come, and the people stand before this house and cry, God will hear and help. The reformed John Gill glosses the "evil" simply as any calamity whatever, the general word under which sword and famine and pestilence are gathered. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott recognizes the verse as a summary of part of Solomon's prayer of dedication in 2 Chronicles 6:24-30, and notes that to appeal to that prayer is itself an act of confidence, since the sign of its acceptance had already been given when fire and glory filled the house at 2 Chronicles 7:1-3. He renders the Hebrew closely: "if there come upon us evil — sword, pestilence, and famine — we will stand before this house and before Thee, for Thy name is in this house, and we will cry unto Thee out of our distress, and Thou shalt hear and save."

Over one word the two grammatical-historical witnesses linger. The term rendered "judgment," shephot, occurs as a noun nowhere else; standing between "sword" and "pestilence" without a conjunction, Ellicott observes, it breaks the symmetry of the sentence and is "probably an ancient gloss," though all the versions carry it and the Vulgate renders "sword of judgment." Keil and Delitzsch agree that the rare word, set between dabar and chereb, denotes a punitive judgment. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it to the same effect: "the sword, or rather the sword of judgement or of vengeance, that is, war, whereby thou punishest thy people for their sins."

The clause "for thy name is in this house" draws a note from Adam Clarke. The wesleyan-arminian commentator records that several of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, with the Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic, add a word so that it reads "thy name is invoked in this house" — "here thou dwellest, and here thou art worshipped"; the Targum renders it "thy Majesty is in this house." The witnesses converge on the point that matters. Gill fixes the breadth of the "evil," Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch the sense and suspect origin of "judgment," Clarke the presence of the invoked name, Wesley the punitive sword. Together they show the king pleading God's own word back to Him: the temple was built precisely for such a day as this, and Jehoshaphat, standing before it, does no more than claim the hearing that was promised when its founder first prayed and the glory came down.
10:
The prayer turns from God's mercies to the injustice of the invaders, and the witnesses draw out the sting in the history it recalls — that these very nations Israel had once been forbidden to touch. The reformed John Gill notes the ancient charge: when Israel came out of Egypt, God would not let them invade Ammon, Moab, or Mount Seir, "charging them not to meddle with them, nor take any of their lands from them." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gathers the several prohibitions — Deuteronomy 2:4, 2:9, and 2:19 — and recalls that Edom had even refused Israel a passage through his territory in Numbers 20:14-21, yet was spared; for these tribes were recognized as the kindred of Israel, being sons of Esau and sons of Lot. He identifies the "children of Mount Seir" here with the Maonites of the opening verse, an Edomite people, and notes that the Syriac reads "mount Gebal," after a tribe of the northern Seir named in Psalms 83:7.

Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the irony that the verse is built upon. "And now" — the contrary of that old forbearance has come to pass. These are the peoples into whose land God would not allow Israel to enter when they came out of Egypt, for under Moses they turned aside from them and destroyed them not, as the record stands in Deuteronomy 2 and Numbers 20; and behold, these same peoples now recompense that ancient mercy by coming to cast Israel out of the possession God had given them.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they expose the moral force of Jehoshaphat's plea. The argument is one of ingratitude turned to aggression. Long ago, at God's own command, Israel had spared the kinsmen through whose borders they passed, forbearing to seize a foot of their land; now those kinsmen, forgetting the debt, march to seize the land God gave His people. Gill fixes the old prohibition, Ellicott the kinship that made it fitting, Keil and Delitzsch the reversal that makes it monstrous. The king is not merely reporting who the enemy is; he is laying their injustice before the Judge of all the earth, asking Him to weigh the contrast between Israel's ancient restraint and the invaders' present cruelty. It is the reasoning that the next verse will press to its conclusion — how they reward us — and that will issue in the direct appeal to God's justice: wilt thou not judge them?
11:
"Behold, how they reward us" — and the witnesses fasten on the bitter equity of the complaint, evil returned for good, and on the peculiar dignity of the land the invaders would seize. The reformed John Gill puts the reward in three words, "evil for good," the exact inversion of Israel's ancient kindness rehearsed in the verse before. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes that six of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, with the Targum, make the charge explicit, reading "behold, they reward us evil" — the word supplied that the sense already demands.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the clause "behold, they are requiting us by coming to drive us out," comparing the confederacy of Psalms 83:4-9; the verb "cast" is the strong word of expulsion used of Adam driven from Eden in Genesis 3:24. He marks a striking phrase: the land is here called "thy possession," a title given the Promised Land nowhere else in the Old Testament, and the clause "thou hast given us to inherit" is literally "madest us possess," the term of Judges 11:24. The point is pressed home by Keil and Delitzsch, who read the whole verse as the hinge of the plea: the peoples Israel once spared now recompense that mercy by coming to cast them out of the possession God Himself had given.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the two grievances into a double appeal to heaven. The enemies, he says, ill requite Israel's ancient kindnesses — God would not let Israel invade them, as Deuteronomy 2:9 forbade — and now they break in upon Israel's ancient rights, coming to seize the land for themselves. "We may comfortably appear to God against those that render us evil for good," Henry observes; and again, of the possession here pleaded, "those that use what they have for God may comfortably hope that he will secure it to them." The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the ingratitude, Ellicott the violence of the expulsion and the unique honour of the land as God's own possession, Keil and Delitzsch the reversal of the old mercy, Henry the twofold ground of confidence it gives. The land is God's grant, held in trust by a people who devote it to Him; and to plead its seizure is to call upon the Landlord to defend His own title against unjust claimants — a plea that runs straight into the cry for judgment that follows.
12:
The prayer ends where it has been tending — in an appeal to God's justice and a confession of utter helplessness. The reformed John Gill reads "wilt thou not judge them?" as a summons to the divine tribunal: bring them to thy bar, examine the charge, convict them of injustice, condemn and punish them for it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it as settled certainty — "thou wilt inflict deserved punishment upon them" — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the rare phrase "exercise judgment upon them," an idiom found here only, comparing "this great company" with the "multitude" of Asa's prayer at 2 Chronicles 14:11.

The confession that follows is what the witnesses prize most. Ellicott renders it "for our part we know not what to do, but our eyes are upon thee": Judah neither knows nor deliberates upon any plan of resistance, for its whole thought is centred upon God and His omnipotence — the very posture of Psalms 25:15, "mine eyes are ever toward the LORD," and of Psalms 123:2. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the historical realism: though Jehoshaphat had great armies, he seems to have been surprised by the invaders before his forces were in readiness, so that the plea of "no might" is no false modesty; and he draws the maxim that "the justice of God is the refuge of those that are wronged."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the closing words into a small anatomy of faith. Jehoshaphat professes his entire dependence upon God for deliverance: though he had a great and well-disciplined army on foot, he said, "we have no might against this great company, none without thee, none to boast of, none to trust to; but our eyes are upon thee." That upward look, Henry says, is "an eye of acknowledgment and humble submission, an eye of faith and entire dependence, an eye of desire and hearty prayer, an eye of hope and patient expectation." The disease seems desperate and they are quite at a loss, yet this is the sovereign remedy. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke and Ellicott fix the appeal to God's judgment, Wesley the reality of the helplessness, Henry the fourfold longing of the eye fixed on heaven. Together they close the prayer on its truest note: a king who has spread the covenant, the land, the sanctuary, and the enemy's injustice before God, and now, disowning all his own strength, casts the whole weight of the crisis upon the God whose justice is the refuge of the wronged and whose power alone can save.
13:
The prayer done, the whole nation stands waiting, and the witnesses dwell on the touching detail that they had brought their families with them. The reformed John Gill pictures all Judah standing before the LORD, "looking towards the most holy place, where the ark of his presence was, in an humble and submissive posture," waiting to see what answer they should have. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the tense — "were standing" — and takes it of the people praying together with their king, perhaps the very assembly remembered in Psalms 48:9, "we have thought of thy lovingkindness, O God, in the midst of thy temple."

The presence of the children moves the other witnesses to their deepest note. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains that the people were wont to present their little ones before the LORD in times of great distress, both to stir up their own more fervent prayers — their eyes resting on their harmless and tender children — and to move God to compassion, since He has declared He will be prevailed with by such methods as these. Keil and Delitzsch record the same fact plainly: they had brought with them their little ones, their wives, and their sons, to pray for deliverance from the enemy.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the scene its voice. They stood before the Lord, he says, "as beggars at his door, with their wives and children"; they and their families were in danger, and therefore they brought their families with them to seek the Lord. Henry even frames their unspoken plea: "Lord, we are indeed a provoking people, that deserve to be abandoned to ruin; but here are little ones that are innocent, let not them perish in the storm." And he recalls the precedent of mercy — Nineveh was spared for the sake of the little ones, as God Himself pleaded at Jonah 4:11. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the humble, waiting posture toward the ark; Ellicott the standing congregation at prayer; Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch the deliberate bringing of the families; Henry the beggar's plea that leans on the innocence of children. Together they render one of the most affecting tableaux in the book: a whole people, from the king to the babe in arms, gathered motionless before the sanctuary, having emptied themselves of every plan and confessed they know not what to do, now simply standing — with their most helpless and beloved beside them — to wait upon the God whose answer is about to come.
14:
The answer breaks in even before the congregation disperses, and the witnesses fix on the man God chose to speak it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marvels at the speed of the mercy: "while he was yet speaking God heard"; before the assembly was dismissed they had assurance of victory, "for it is never in vain to seek God." The spirit of prophecy came upon a Levite who stood not in any place of eminency "but in the midst of the congregation" — and Henry draws the lesson from the very obscurity of the vessel: "the Spirit, like the wind, blows where and on whom he listeth." Jahaziel was of the sons of Asaph, one of the singers, and on that office God would thus put an honour; whether he had been a prophet before is uncertain, though most probably he was.

The grammatical-historical witnesses trace his lineage with care. Charles Ellicott renders the Hebrew "upon Jahaziel there fell the spirit," the same idiom as the "spirit of courage from the LORD" in 2 Chronicles 15:1, and notes that this Levitical musician is named nowhere else, his pedigree carried back five generations to a Mattaniah who should probably be read Nethaniah, a son of Asaph contemporary with David in 1 Chronicles 25:2. Keil and Delitzsch reason the genealogy the same way: the Mattaniah at its head is not the Hemanite of 1 Chronicles 25:4, but perhaps the Asaphite Nethaniah of 1 Chronicles 25:12, since the letters mem and nun are easily confounded; and in the midst of the assembly the Spirit of the LORD came upon him to promise king and people miraculous help. The reformed John Gill simply sets down the names of the five generations, Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, the son of Benaiah, the son of Jeiel, the son of Mattaniah, anchoring the prophet in a real and traceable Levitical house rather than leaving him a nameless voice.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the lineage, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch refine it and mark the descent from Asaph the singer, Henry reads the theology of the choice. That the word of deliverance should fall not on the king, nor on a priest at the altar, but on a temple-singer standing anonymous in the crowd, is itself part of the message: the God who cannot be withstood answers a praying people through whatever instrument He pleases, and honours the humble ministry of song by making one of its number the mouth of prophecy in Judah's hour of need.
15:
The prophet's word begins with a summons and a reversal — the battle is not Judah's but God's. The reformed John Gill hears in the address a rising climax: "all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat," mounting from the people of the country towns, to the citizens of the metropolis, to the supreme governor himself, so that none is left out of the comfort. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the opening "hearken ye" beside the prophetic calls of Isaiah 49:1 and 51:4, and the charge "be not afraid nor dismayed" beside Deuteronomy 1:21.

The heart of the oracle is the great sentence, "the battle is not yours, but God's." Keil and Delitzsch gloss it directly: you have not to make war upon this multitude, for the Lord will do it — the same confession David had flung at Goliath, "the battle is the LORD's," in 1 Samuel 17:47. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the point to its edge: "God will not employ you in the discomfiture of this great host; he himself will take the matter in hand, deliver you, and destroy them." Ellicott enriches it with the divine name behind it — Jehovah Sabaoth, the LORD of the hosts of Israel — and observes that it was on the battlefield that Jehovah's presence was most clearly realized, the very truth the psalmists sing when they cry, "the LORD of hosts is with us," in Psalms 46:7.

The witnesses do not divide, and the sentence they gather around overturns every ordinary calculation of war. Judah had confessed in its prayer, "we have no might against this great company"; the prophet answers that its might was never the point, for the company is God's to deal with, not theirs. The great multitude that had filled the king with fear is here named again — the "great company" of the prayer — only to be handed over to a greater. Gill marks how the word reaches every rank of the trembling nation, Ellicott sets it in the long line of prophetic encouragement and in the title of the LORD of hosts, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke fix its plain meaning that God Himself will fight. The people who came knowing not what to do are told they need do nothing in the way of battle at all; the war has been lifted off their shoulders and taken up by the God who cannot be withstood. What remains is only to go where He directs and to see — the theme the next verses unfold.
16:
The prophecy grows precise, naming the road the enemy climbs and the place Judah will find them. The reformed John Gill explains the order to "go down": the present day was the fast, no fit time to march, but on the morrow they might go out with great confidence, and since Jerusalem stood on an eminence they are bidden descend toward the foe. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way — "go down from Jerusalem, where he and his army now were, which stood upon high ground."

The grammatical-historical witnesses labour over the topography. Charles Ellicott renders "they come up by the cliff of Ziz" as "they are ascending by the ascent of Hazziz," a pass or mountain path leading up from Engedi to the desert table-land; "the brook" is a wady or ravine, and "the wilderness of Jeruel," though its name is now unknown, appears from comparing v.2 and v.20 to be the great stretch of waste since called el Husasah, from a wady on its northern side. Keil and Delitzsch describe that country from Robinson's survey — a high table-land sloping gradually eastward, wholly waste, bounded on the south by its wady and reaching from the Dead Sea toward Tekoa; the "height of Hazziz," they add, has perhaps left its trace in the modern Wady el Hasasah, and the Septuagint transcribes the name as Asseis.

The witnesses do not divide; they simply pool their maps. What matters in their agreement is the exactness of the promise. The prophet does not merely tell Judah that God will fight; he tells them the very ascent by which the invaders will climb from the oasis of Engedi and the very end of the valley where they will be found, so that when the men of Judah march out on the morrow they go not into uncertainty but to a rendezvous already fixed by the word of God. Gill and Wesley account for the descent from the high city; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch settle the pass, the ravine, and the waste table-land where the confrontation is appointed. The effect is to bind the coming deliverance tightly to prophecy: the place is named beforehand, so that the outcome, when it comes, will be seen to be no accident of war but the keeping of a word spoken in the temple court the day before, and every step of the march a walking into fulfilment.
17:
The command reaches its climax in a paradox — an army told it need not fight. The reformed John Gill states the ground in a phrase: they "shall not need to fight in this battle," since the Lord would fight for them. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole charge closely: "ye have not to fight herein; only come hither, stand, and see the help of the LORD with you" — you need do nothing more, and therefore need not fear. The battle already declared to be God's is now formally lifted from Judah's hands; their part is reduced to presence and sight.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the verbs. "It is not for you to fight," he renders, comparing 1 Chronicles 15:2; "set yourselves" means station yourselves, take your stand, and the following "stand ye still" looks like an explanatory addition, perhaps a marginal gloss. Above all he hears the deliberate echo of the Exodus: "fear not, take your stand, and see the salvation of the LORD" is almost word for word the command of Moses to Israel at the Red Sea in Exodus 14:13, just before the great deliverance. The battle by the desert of Jeruel is cast as a second Red Sea, where the people stand and watch God overthrow their pursuers.

Over the last clause, "the LORD with you," Ellicott offers two readings and inclines to one. It might be a divine title — "the LORD-with-you," on the pattern of Immanuel, "with us God," in Isaiah 7:14 — but more probably the stop falls at "the LORD," and "with you, O Judah and Jerusalem" is an elliptic promise that He is, or will be, with them, as in 2 Chronicles 19:6. Either way the sense answers the refrain of the Korahite psalm, "the LORD of hosts is with us." The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the reason, Keil and Delitzsch the reduction of Judah's task to standing and seeing, Ellicott the Red Sea pattern and the promise of God's presence. Together they complete the great overturning of the chapter: a people who marched out in fear are told that fear is now needless, that the sword may stay in its sheath, and that all their warfare in this instance is to take their stand and behold the salvation their God will work — the very command their fathers obeyed on the shore of the sea, and the same deliverance now pledged in the wilderness.
18:
The oracle draws from king and people an immediate act of worship, and the witnesses read the gesture as faith answering the promise. The reformed John Gill notes that Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground "not only in reverence of God, and his prophet, but as a token of his belief of what was said, and his thankfulness for it" — the posture is not mere ceremony but assent. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the scene precisely: the king "bowed, face earthward," while all the people prostrated themselves upon their faces, both alike "to do worship to Jehovah," the very attitude of adoration seen when the glory appeared in Leviticus 9:24, of Joshua before the captain of the LORD's host in Joshua 5:14, and of David when the destroying angel stood over Jerusalem in 1 Chronicles 21:16.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the movement that the worship sets going: for this comforting assurance the king and people thanked the Lord, falling down before Him, whereupon the Levites stood up to praise God with a loud voice — the singers of the house of Kohath, and specially the Korahites descended from him, as their line is traced in 1 Chronicles 6:22. The bowing of the whole nation is thus the pivot between the promise and the praise that will carry them into the field.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the act its inward voice. They bowed their heads, he says, Jehoshaphat first and then all the people, and fell before the Lord and worshipped, "receiving with a holy awe and fear of God this token of his favour, and saying with faith, Be it unto us according to thy word." That last phrase is the key Henry turns: the worship is the amen of faith, a people accepting a victory not yet seen as though it were already given. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the belief and thankfulness in the bow, Ellicott the depth of the prostration and its Old Testament precedents, Keil and Delitzsch the rising of the Levites it prompts, Henry the faith that says "be it unto us according to thy word." Together they show a remarkable order: the answer to the prayer is met not with cheering, nor with a rush to arms, but with the whole congregation on its face before God. Before ever they see the salvation promised, they worship the God who promised it — the surest sign that they have truly believed the prophet's word, and the seed of the strange, singing march that the next verses will describe.
19:
The worship of the prostrate nation rises into song as the Levites take their feet, and the witnesses attend to who these singers were and what their standing meant. The reformed John Gill identifies them as the posterity of Kohath in the line of Korah. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines the pedigree: "sons of the Kohathites" specifies the clan, "sons of the Korhites" the particular house of the musicians who rose on this occasion — the Korahites being the leading division of Kohath in 1 Chronicles 6:22, and the "and" that joins them explanatory, meaning "even, namely, some of the sons of Korah." These, he notes, were a guild of Levitical minstrels of the first rank, remembered in the headings of many psalms, such as the forty-fourth through the forty-ninth, that bear their name; and they "stood up to praise the LORD God of Israel," the word being the hallel of 1 Chronicles 16:14.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the two small phrases for their weight of faith. They stood up "by Jehoshaphat's appointment," he says, and praised "on high" — that is, with heart and voice lifted up together — whereby they showed "their full assurance of the victory." The loudness is not excitement but confidence: men do not shout a triumph-song over a battle unfought unless they wholly believe the word that has promised it.

Keil and Delitzsch carry the scene into the next morning, for the Levites' praise is the overture to the march. The singers, they note, were the first to break forth in thanksgiving; and on the morrow the assembled men of Judah rose early and went out toward the wilderness, Jehoshaphat standing to counsel them to trust firmly in the LORD and His prophets, as at Isaiah 7:9, before ordering them to march — not to fight, but to assure themselves of the wonderful help of the Lord. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the line of Korah, Ellicott the rank of the minstrel-guild and the temple word for their praise, Wesley the lifted heart that betokened assurance, Keil and Delitzsch the praise as the threshold of the march. Together they show the astonishing thing the chapter is building toward: an army whose vanguard is a choir, whose first weapon is a hymn, and whose Levites, appointed to no rampart but to a song, lift up the loud praise of the God of Israel over a victory they have believed before they have seen.
20:
The march sets out, and at its head Jehoshaphat preaches a sermon of one text — believe, and be established. The reformed John Gill notes that they rose early, confident of success and animated by what the prophet had said. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the king's strange muster: instead of calling his men to handle their arms and keep their ranks, "he bade them believe in the Lord God and give credit to his word in the mouth of his prophets," and assured them they should prosper and be established. Faith, Henry says, was to be their armour: "that is true courage which faith inspires a man with; nor will any thing contribute more to the establishing of the heart in shaking times than a firm belief of the power, and mercy, and promise of God." In our spiritual conflicts too, he adds, "this is the victory, even our faith."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the exhortation a deliberate reversal of an old prophecy. "Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established" is the affirmative form of Isaiah's warning to Ahaz, "if ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established," in Isaiah 7:9 — the very words turned from threat to promise. He places the scene geographically: the host went forth into the wilderness of Tekoa, part of the desert of Jeruel, Tekoa lying about ten miles south of Jerusalem and commanding a view over the table-land of el Husasah, while the king "stood," or came forward, probably in the gate of the city, to speak.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fix the objects of the faith. John Wesley takes "believe his prophets" of God's promise delivered by Jahaziel, and consequently of all the prophet's predictions. Adam Clarke lingers, as ever, on the Targum, which renders "believe in the Word of the LORD your God, and believe in his law, and believe in his prophets, and ye shall prosper" — where, he says, "the Word and the revelation are most pointedly distinguished, the Word being used personally," a hint of the divine Logos. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the early, animated start, Henry the doctrine that faith is the soldier's true armour, Ellicott the reversal of Isaiah's word and the ground the army crossed, Wesley and Clarke the double object of belief — the LORD Himself and the prophet He sent. Together they show a king leading men into a wilderness not with a battle-plan but with a creed, staking the fate of the kingdom on whether Judah will simply believe.
21:
The council of war ends in a decision without parallel — to send singers in front of the soldiers. The reformed John Gill takes the king's consultation with the people as a conference with his principal officers on the order of the march and the array they should keep. But the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the sense of "consulted": the word is rather "advised" or "warned," gave counsel to the people, as in 2 Kings 6:8; and the phrase "praise the beauty of holiness" he would render "men praising in holy apparel" — that is, in the Levitical vestments of 1 Chronicles 16:29 and Psalms 29:2. Their cry, "Praise the LORD, for his mercy endureth for ever," is the great temple refrain of 2 Chronicles 5:13, and this band of minstrels was to march before the armed host, as the trumpet-priests had gone before the ark at Jericho in Joshua 6:7.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley, in nearly the same words, unfold the strangeness of the tactic. Jehoshaphat called a council of war, and it was resolved to appoint singers to go out before the army, "to charge in the front, who had nothing else to do but to praise God" — to praise His holiness, which is His beauty, with that ancient doxology "which eternity itself will not wear thread-bare." By this strange advance to the field, Henry says, the king expressed his firm reliance on the word of God, which enabled him to triumph before the battle; he meant to animate his own soldiers, to confound the enemy, and to engage God on their side, "for praise pleases God better than all burnt offering and sacrifice."

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the counsel and the vestured choir with its temple refrain, Keil and Delitzsch note that the singing was the signal for the ambush God would set, and Henry and Wesley read the theology of a vanguard of praise. Together they display the boldest stroke of faith in the chapter: an army that puts its worshippers where its shock-troops should be, and marches to war behind men whose only weapon is the confession that God's mercy endures for ever. The choir set in the van is the visible creed of the king who commanded it: he has believed the prophet's word so wholly that he treats the victory as already won, and orders the thanksgiving before the enemy is so much as seen. The praise is at once the proof of Judah's belief and, as the next verse will show, the appointed moment at which the LORD Himself strikes.
22:
At the sound of the first hymn the enemy is undone, and the witnesses converge on the fact while dividing sharply over the means. The reformed John Gill pictures the singers swelling their praise as they neared the foe. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, fixes the timing: "at the very time when they began with shouting and praise," having reached the neighbourhood of the enemy, their joyful paean became the signal for a divine interposition, as the shout at Jericho had been in Joshua 6:20; the "ambushments" are "liers in wait" (the word of Judges 9:25), and "they were smitten" anticipates the slaughter the next verse details.

How the confederates destroyed themselves is the true question, and here the witnesses part. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley offers two possibilities: either the liers in wait were holy angels, appearing in the shape of men and even wearing the visages of Moabites and Ammonites, who slew the rest — so that each part, supposing the slaughter done by its own allies, fell upon the others; or else God simply "raised jealousies and animosities among themselves" that broke into open war. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry balances the same two options, hosts of angels or, with Bishop Patrick, "their own ambushments, whom God struck with such confusion that they fell upon their own friends as if they had been enemies"; and he marks the timing devotionally — God did this "when his people began to sing and to praise, for he delights to furnish those with matter for praise that have hearts for it." Adam Clarke, following Houbigant and the Targum, reads a chain: God set the men of Mount Seir in ambush, Ammon and Moab were smitten, then turned on Seir and destroyed it, and then fell upon one another.

Ellicott presses hardest for a wholly natural sequence. The self-destruction was providential, he insists, but need not have been miraculous; angels would have been named more plainly, and the Judeans were mere spectators, not an ambush. Most likely some portion of the straggling host was suddenly set upon by a lurking band of Bedouin freebooters; the partial confusion swelled into universal panic; Ammon and Moab suspected their wilder Maonite allies of treachery and fell upon them, then, maddened by slaughter and old feuds, upon each other — a self-annihilation like that of the Midianites thrown into confusion by Gideon in Judges 7:22. The prophet, he adds, foresaw the issue but not the course, just as Elisha foretold plenty to famished Samaria in 2 Kings 7. So the debate stands: were the "liers in wait" angelic executioners, or a natural panic providentially arranged? Wesley and Henry hold both open; Ellicott argues firmly for the second; but none doubts that, at the note of praise, God Himself turned the invaders' swords upon their own ranks.
23:
The verse names the mechanism of the ruin — the allies turning on one another — and the witnesses trace the grim sequence. The reformed John Gill explains the first blow: the children of Ammon and Moab "stood up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir," supposing that these had played them false and gone over to the enemy's side. Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, follow the carnage to its end: Ammon and Moab rose up to slay and utterly destroy the men of Seir, "and when they had made an end of the inhabitants of Seir, every one helped to destroy another" — the survivors turning their swords upon their own confederates.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, sharpens the vocabulary of the slaughter. "Stood up against" is a late idiom, the same construction found in 1 Chronicles 21:1; "utterly to slay" is the strong word to devote to destruction, to place under the ban; and the closing clause is literally "they helped, each against his fellow, for destruction," the term of ruin used in Ezekiel 5:16. Every phrase, in his reading, deepens the picture of an army consuming itself.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the theology out of the wreckage. The Ammonites and Moabites fell foul upon the Edomites and cut them off, and then they fell out with one another and cut one another off; "thus God often makes wicked people instruments of destruction to one another," and "what alliances can be so firm as to keep those together whom God designs to dash in pieces one against another?" Those are wretchedly infatuated to their ruin, Henry adds, "that fall foul upon their friends as if they were enemies." The witnesses do not divide. Gill supplies the spark of suspicion, Keil and Delitzsch the order of the killing, Ellicott the ferocity of its language, Henry the lesson that God can arm His enemies against themselves. Together they show the promise of the previous day fulfilled to the letter: Judah was told it would not need to fight, and here the vast confederacy, needing no sword of Judah's, destroys itself utterly in the wilderness. The league that had marched so confidently from beyond the sea dissolves in mutual massacre, and the only hand that moved against it was its own — moved, the chapter insists, by the God who set the ambush at the sound of praise.
24:
Judah reaches the look-out and sees the work already done. The reformed John Gill supposes the watch-tower stood on the hill or cliff of Ziz, set there for the direction of travellers and their protection from robbers. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley locates it the same way — upon the cliff of Ziz named in v.16 — and adds that it looked out toward the wilderness where the enemy lay encamped, so that from it Judah could descry the invaders' numbers, order, and condition.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the moment and the sight. Charles Ellicott renders "now Judah had come," by the time the slaughter was complete, "toward the watch tower," the look-out of the desert, the mizpeh that means watch-tower in Isaiah 21:8; and there "they looked," and behold, dead bodies fallen to the earth — a spectacle like the Assyrian camp of corpses in 2 Kings 19:35 — with no survivor anywhere visible. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same approach: when Judah came to the height in the wilderness of Tekoa, whence one might look out over the desert of Jeruel, and turned toward the multitude of the enemy — the very multitude of the prayer in v.12 — they saw corpses in such number lying there that, to all appearance, none had escaped.

The witnesses do not divide, and the restraint of their comment matches the stillness of the scene. Judah had marched out expecting, at most, to stand and watch a battle; they arrive to find the battle over and the field a carpet of the slain. The great host that had filled the king with fear, that the prophet had named a "great multitude," that the prayer had confessed Judah powerless to face, lies dead to the last man before a single sword of Judah's has been drawn. Gill and Wesley set the tower on its cliff above the waste, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch fix the look-out and the appalling view from it — bodies fallen, none escaped. Together they mark the exact fulfilment of the word "ye shall not need to fight": the men of Judah come to the edge of the wilderness only to look down upon the salvation of the LORD already accomplished, and to learn that the God who bade them stand still has, in the night, emptied the field of every enemy. Nothing remains of the great confederacy but the plunder the next verse will gather.
25:
The victory becomes a harvest, and the witnesses divide, mildly, over one word in the inventory of spoil while marvelling together at its abundance. The reformed John Gill notes that all Judah had to do now was to gather plunder — "they had no need to fight, the Lord had fought for them." The received text says they found among the fallen "riches with the dead bodies, and precious jewels"; but the mention of corpses in the midst of the treasure struck the witnesses as strange. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports that eight manuscripts and several ancient editions read begadim, "garments," for pegarim, "dead bodies" — the two words easily confused — and that no version but the Chaldee has "dead bodies"; he judges "garments" the true reading. Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, lean the same way: "garments," set beside movable wealth and costly vessels, suits the list far better than corpses. So the debate is textual and real — did Judah strip clothing, or ornaments from the slain? — though it touches only a word, not the fact of the plunder.

Ellicott adds further refinements: the Septuagint reads "cattle" for "among them," so that they found herds in abundance; "precious jewels" is literally "vessels of desirable things," costly articles; and "more than they could carry away" is literally "until there was no loading," the spoil so vast that they were three days in gathering it. He and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley account for such riches by the character of the invasion: the confederates had come intending a permanent settlement, and so, as the prayer had said in v.11, brought all their goods with them — jewels, Wesley suggests, to corrupt officials or buy provisions, coming "as to triumph rather than to fight," puffed up by God to their own destruction.

Ellicott lifts the scene at last to prophecy. The overthrow was so great that the prophet Joel makes it a type of the final judgment of Israel's enemies in the "valley of Jehoshaphat," a name that alludes at once to this catastrophe and to the truth that "Jehovah is judge," in Joel 3:12. The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Gill fixes the effortless gathering, Clarke and the grammatical-historical voices weigh garments against corpses, Wesley explains the wealth, Ellicott crowns it with Joel's vision. Together they show a people enriched by an enemy who came to dispossess them — three days stripping the field where they had feared to die, and carrying home, as pure gift, the plunder of a host they never fought.
26:
On the fourth day the army turns aside to bless the God who had blessed it, and the witnesses gather around the place and its abiding name. The reformed John Gill notes that they assembled in the valley of Berachah, "so called from what they did there" — the name a memorial of the act. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it plainly: Berachah is the Hebrew for blessing, given the valley "from their solemn blessings and praises given to God in it upon this occasion," and Adam Clarke adds that the Targum renders it "the valley of Benediction."

The grammatical-historical witnesses locate the spot on the modern map. Keil and Delitzsch explain that on the fourth day the men of Judah gathered to give thanks for the deliverance in a valley not far from the battle-field, which thence received the name "valley of blessing"; the ancient name still survives in the Wady Bereikut, west of Tekoa, near the road that leads from Hebron to Jerusalem, where Robinson found ruins covering three or four acres, and which Jerome had mentioned long before. Charles Ellicott confirms the identification — the wide, open Wady Beraikut — and recalls that Jerome speaks of a Caphar Barucha, a "village of blessing," in the same neighbourhood. The closing formula, "unto this day," Ellicott notes, is a notice after the manner of the ancient historians, like the naming of Bethel in Genesis 28:19 and of Massah in Exodus 17:7.

The witnesses do not divide, and their agreement lets the verse do its commemorative work. The army that had marched out singing does not disperse the moment the danger is past; it pauses, on the very ground of its rescue, to render thanks, and by that thanksgiving stamps a name on the land itself. Gill and Wesley and Clarke fix the meaning of the name, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the valley that still bears its trace and the historian's formula that preserves it. Together they show how deliberately the deliverance was to be remembered: a valley of blessing set in the wilderness, so that every later traveller on the Hebron road might ask its name and be told the story of the day when Judah went out to war with a hymn and came back with a benediction. The place of thanksgiving is fixed in the earth, a standing witness, the Chronicler means, for the encouragement of every generation that would learn to trust the God who fights for those who praise Him.
27:
The march home is as joyful as the march out was believing, and the witnesses dwell on the king at the head of a rejoicing people. The reformed John Gill notes that they returned to Jerusalem to praise the LORD in the temple, as they had already praised Him in the valley — the thanksgiving carried from the field into the sanctuary. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders "in the forefront of them" as "at their head," and observes that they went back "as they came, in festal procession"; the phrase "the LORD had made them to rejoice over their enemies" is the same used of the restored exiles in Ezra 6:22 and Nehemiah 12:43.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes on Jehoshaphat's place in the column and makes it a portrait of leadership. The king went "in the forefront of them" — "he was their leader," Clarke says, "in all these spiritual, holy, fatiguing, and self-denying exercises. What a noble and persuasive pattern!" The monarch who had led the fast, led the prayer, and led the march now leads the procession of praise, first in devotion as he was first in rank.

Keil and Delitzsch set the return in its larger frame: they came back with Jehoshaphat at their head, with joy, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies, and went up with the music of the Levites and priests to the house of God; and they add that this wonderful deliverance was very likely the theme of the Korahite psalms, the forty-sixth, forty-seventh, and forty-eighth, and perhaps of the eighty-third, composed by an Asaphite — possibly by Jahaziel himself. The witnesses do not divide. Gill carries the praise from valley to temple, Ellicott fixes the festal order of the return, Clarke holds up the king as the pattern of a leader foremost in worship, Keil and Delitzsch hear the whole event echoing in the psalter. Together they complete the rhythm the chapter has kept throughout: the people who went out singing come back singing, and their joy is not the ordinary elation of victors — for they won no battle — but the rejoicing of men whom the LORD Himself has made glad over enemies they never struck. The procession that had gone down to the wilderness in faith returns to the holy city in triumph, its king at its head, to lay its thanksgiving where it had first laid its prayer.
28:
The rejoicing procession enters the city to the sound of instruments, and the witnesses attend to the music and the meaning of praise that will not cease. The reformed John Gill names the three principal instruments used in the singing of God's praises — psalteries, harps, and trumpets — and pictures them sounding as the returning host came to Jerusalem, entered it, and passed through. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines the rendering to "harps, guitars, and clarions," and suggests that the forty-seventh psalm, with its summons "sing praises to God, sing praises," may well commemorate this very procession to the temple, in Psalms 47:6. Keil and Delitzsch simply record the destination: they came with their music "unto the house of the LORD," the sanctuary that had been the scene of the prayer now becoming the scene of the praise.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws from the return a lesson on the perpetuity of thanksgiving. They came to the house of God, he says, "to renew their praises in the court of the temple, the proper and usual place for it"; and he presses the point home: "praising God must not be the work of a day only, but our praises, when we have received mercy, must be often repeated, as our prayers were when we were in pursuit of it. Every day we must bless God; as long as we live, and while we have any being, we must praise him, spending our time in that work in which we hope to spend our eternity."

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse closes the circle of the chapter. The temple where Judah had stood as beggars at the door, crying "we know not what to do," is the temple to which they now return in triumph with harp and trumpet; the place of the petition becomes the place of the thanksgiving. Gill names the instruments of the joy, Ellicott hears it echoed in the psalter, Keil and Delitzsch mark its sanctuary destination, Wesley turns it into a call for unwearied, lifelong praise. Together they show that the deliverance is not complete until it is brought back, in music, to the God who gave it. The mercy obtained by prayer in that house is now acknowledged by praise in the same house — for, as Wesley says, thanksgiving is the earthly rehearsal of an eternal employment, and Judah, marching into the temple with its instruments, is doing on its glad day what the redeemed will do for ever.
29:
The report of the deliverance spreads terror through the surrounding nations, and the witnesses read that dread as the visible sign that God had fought. The reformed John Gill takes "the fear of God" to have fallen upon all the kingdoms of those countries whose armies had been slain, and upon the neighbouring lands besides. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders it "a divine dread fell upon all the kingdoms of the countries round Judah," the same terror noted in 2 Chronicles 17:10 and sung in Psalms 48:7, "fear took hold upon them there." That the LORD had fought for His people, he adds, was evident from the catastrophe that had befallen their enemies; and he draws a fine theological point — the warfare of the divine Being was seen "not apart from, but in a course of events, which, however natural, was almost as marvellous as a visible intervention of angelic hosts."

Keil and Delitzsch mark the twofold effect: the fame of this victory of the LORD over the enemies of Israel spread the terror of God over all the kingdoms of the lands, and in consequence the kingdom of Judah had rest, as it had after an earlier deliverance in 2 Chronicles 17:10. The dread abroad purchases the peace at home.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the awe of the neighbours. When they heard that God fought thus for Israel, he says, they could not but own, "there is none like unto the God of Jeshurun," and the report "begat in the neighbours a reverence of God and a cautious fear of doing any injury to his people; it is dangerous fighting against those who have God with them." The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the reach of the fear, Ellicott its character as the proof of God's own warfare hidden within natural events, Keil and Delitzsch the rest it bought, Henry the reverence it stirred. Together they show that the miracle by the desert of Jeruel did more than save Judah for a day; it published abroad the name of the God who fights for His people, so that the very nations that had despised Jehoshaphat for his alliance with Ahab now feared to touch the kingdom his God defended. The dread of the LORD, spread over the surrounding peoples, becomes the wall around a realm that had gone to war with nothing but a prayer and a song.
30:
The chapter's deliverance issues in peace, and the witnesses weigh the rest that God gave and its double character. The reformed John Gill reads the quiet as both inward and outward: the realm of Jehoshaphat was at peace "among themselves, and none from abroad dared to molest them." Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, ground that peace where the text does — "for his God gave him rest round about" — and note that with this the Chronicler brings his account of the reign toward its close, gathering the concluding notices that answer to the fuller record in 1 Kings 22:41-51. Charles Ellicott observes that the same rest had been said of Asa's kingdom in 2 Chronicles 14:6 and 2 Chronicles 15:15, and compares the recurring notices in Judges of the quiet that followed the overthrow of a national enemy, as in Judges 3:30 — the land having rest a set number of years.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the two sides of the quiet. The kingdom was made very easy at home, he says, first quiet among themselves: those who had been displeased at Jehoshaphat's destroying of the images and groves were now satisfied, "obliged to own that since the God of Israel could deliver after this sort, he only is to be worshipped, in that way only which he himself has appointed." And second, quiet from the fear of insults from their neighbours, "God having given them rest round about. And, if he give rest, who can give disturbance?"

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the peace within and without, Keil and Delitzsch its ground in God's gift and its place at the reign's summing-up, Ellicott its likeness to the rest of Asa and the judges, Henry its twofold fruit — a people reconciled to the reformation and a border safe from assault. Together they close the great narrative of the invasion on the note of Sabbath. The war that opened in fear and a proclaimed fast ends in a realm at rest, and the rest is expressly God's doing, not the fruit of arms Judah never used. The chapter that began with an enemy already at Engedi ends with a kingdom quiet on every side; and the lesson the witnesses leave is Henry's — that the peace which God bestows no power on earth can break, for if He gives rest, who can give disturbance?
31:
The narrative turns from the great deliverance to the formal summary of the reign, and the witnesses read the closing notices against their parallel in the older history. The reformed John Gill treats the verse as matter already told, referring the reader to the corresponding record in 1 Kings 22:41 and following, where Jehoshaphat's age, the length of his reign, and his mother's name are given. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the comparison exact: the book of Kings adds that he began to reign "in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel," and with that single omission the Chronicler's verse coincides with 1 Kings 22:41-42 — Jehoshaphat thirty-five years old at his accession, reigning twenty-five years in Jerusalem, his mother Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. Keil and Delitzsch note that these concluding notes answer throughout to the account in 1 Kings 22:41-51, the two records agreeing on the king's age, the length and the character of his reign, though the Chronicler will presently substitute for the stereotyped formula about the high places a remark more searching about the people's hearts.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the bare regnal notice into a verdict on the whole reign. We are now drawing toward the close of Jehoshaphat's history, he says, the fuller record of which was kept in the authentic history written by Jehu the prophet, named in 2 Chronicles 19:2 and still extant when this book was published. The general character of the reign, Henry judges, was that "he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, kept close to the worship of God himself, and did what he could to keep his people close to it" — a reign, on the whole, of piety and reformation. Yet two shadows remain, which the following verses will name: the people's lingering fondness for the high places, and the king's own fatal fondness for the house of Ahab.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill defers to the parallel, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch fix the exact agreement of the two accounts and the one telling divergence to come, Henry pronounces the reign's essential goodness while marking the flaws that will darken its end. Together they open the epilogue of a long and, in the main, faithful reign — a king thirty-five at his crowning and twenty-five years on the throne, whose deliverance the chapter has just celebrated, and whose closing record will now weigh his genuine devotion against the two entanglements he could never quite shake off.
32:
The Chronicler's verdict on the king's walk is brief but weighty — he followed his father Asa and turned not aside from the right. The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the wording and its parallel. Charles Ellicott notes that where the Chronicler writes "he walked in the way of Asa his father," the book of Kings has "all the way," and that the pronoun in "departed not from it" is here feminine where Kings has it masculine, the same small variation seen in 2 Chronicles 17:3; the closing "doing that which was right" he renders "so as to do" the right, marking it as the fruit and evidence of that steady walk. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse together with the notice that follows, as the settled formula of a good reign: Jehoshaphat kept to his father's course, departed not from it, and did what was right in the sight of the LORD.

The comparison with Asa is the heart of the commendation. To walk "in the way of Asa" is to be measured against the reformer who had put away idols and sought the LORD, and the Chronicler's point is that Jehoshaphat, so far from declining from his father, held the same path — a continuity of devotion from one generation to the next. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, summing the reign in these closing verses, gives the same character its fuller weight: Jehoshaphat "did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, kept close to the worship of God himself, and did what he could to keep his people close to it." The verse, on his reading, is no empty formula but a true testimony to a life of piety maintained.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the text and its differences from the older record, Keil and Delitzsch set the verse as the standing verdict of a faithful king, Henry fills out what that faithfulness meant in practice. Together they render the Chronicler's essential judgment upon Jehoshaphat: that he belonged to the better line of Judah's kings, the son who did not squander his father's reformation but carried it on. Yet the very next word — "howbeit" — will remind the reader that even a reign so commended was not without its unreformed corners; the good walk was real, but it left the high places standing, and the faithful king had faults the honest historian will not hide. The commendation of this verse, then, is genuine but not unqualified, the bright ground against which the shadows of the following verses fall.
33:
The first shadow on the reign is the survival of the high places, and the witnesses labour to reconcile it with an earlier notice that Jehoshaphat had removed them. The reformed John Gill draws the distinction on which the harmony turns: the high places where idols had been worshipped were taken away, but not those where sacrifices were offered to the true God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states it as a rule: this is no contradiction of 2 Chronicles 17:6, where Jehoshaphat "took away the high places" — there the holy places of heathenism are meant, here the places of the illegal, if well-intended, worship of Jehovah outside the temple. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same way: the idolatry was universally suppressed, but some of the sites where it had been practised were left standing, and these, to so fickle a people, became the means of idolatry again in reigns less friendly to true religion.

The witnesses agree, too, on where the blame lay. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley insists the high places were not removed "universally," and that the fault was "not in Jehoshaphat, but in the people, who, though they did worship the true God, yet would not be confined to the temple, but for their own conveniency, or from their affection to their ancient custom, chose to worship him in the high places." Keil and Delitzsch find the Chronicler's own diagnosis in the clause that follows: the people "had not yet determinedly turned their heart to the God of their fathers" — a remark he sets in place of the stereotyped formula of Kings.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the point into a lesson on half-hearted reformation. The people retained a partiality for the high places, he says; Jehoshaphat was loth to disoblige them so far as to take these away, "for as yet they had not prepared their hearts to serve the God of their fathers." They complied with his reformation because they could not for shame do otherwise, but they were not hearty in it, "did not direct their hearts to God" — and "the best magistrates cannot bring to pass what they would, in reformation, when the people are cool in it." The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott and Clarke reconcile the notice with the earlier removal, Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch and Henry locate the failure in the people's unprepared hearts. Together they mark the limit of even a good king's reforming zeal: he could pull down the shrines of false gods, but he could not, against a lukewarm people, confine the worship of the true God to the one place He had chosen.
34:
The reign is remitted to its fuller chronicle, and the witnesses attend to the lost book named as its source. The reformed John Gill notes that the "rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last," are those done at the beginning and at the latter end of his reign — the whole compass of a life now referred elsewhere.
