The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the melancholy fact that this record, "the book of Jehu," is "totally lost, though it is evident that it was in being when the books of Chronicles were written" — a vanished source the Chronicler could still consult.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the notice beside its parallel. The book of Kings, at 1 Kings 22:45, refers the reader to "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah" for Jehoshaphat's acts, "and his might that he shewed, and how he warred" — and that last phrase, Ellicott observes, "hints at his victory over the three allies" this very chapter has told. He renders "the book" more literally "the words," and "who is mentioned" as "which is inscribed" or entered in the book of the kings of Israel; "the words of Jehu the son of Hanani" is the title of a prophetic monograph, here said to have been incorporated into that larger work. Keil and Delitzsch read the reference the same way — the fuller acts of the reign written in the book of Jehu the son of Hanani, which was taken up into the book of the kings of Israel.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out who this Jehu was and why his authorship matters. The history was written by "Jehu the prophet" — the same seer who had met Jehoshaphat returning from Ramoth-gilead and rebuked his alliance with Ahab, named in 2 Chronicles 19:2 — a record still extant when the book of Chronicles was published. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the scope of the "first and last," Clarke laments the book's loss, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch trace its title and its absorption into the royal annals, Henry identifies its prophetic author. Together they show the Chronicler's method and his sources: he does not pretend to tell all, but points the reader to the fuller monograph of a prophet who had known the king and dealt faithfully with him — the same prophet whose warning against ungodly alliances the closing verses of the chapter are about to prove tragically justified.
35:
The last and gravest shadow falls: after all God's mercies, Jehoshaphat allies himself with a wicked king of Israel. The reformed John Gill fixes the aggravation in the timing — "after this" means not merely after the invasion, but after Jehoshaphat had returned from Ramoth-gilead and been reproved by a prophet for helping the ungodly; that so soon after such a rebuke he should join himself to a wicked prince, though in trade and not in war, was a great instance of his folly and weakness, the more so since Ahaziah reigned but two short years. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the chronology: since Ahaziah began to reign in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat and reigned two years, as 1 Kings 22:51 records, the league must have been formed in the seventeenth or eighteenth year of the king of Judah. He notes that the Chronicler has passed over the notice that "Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel" in 1 Kings 22:44, and that his account, peculiar to Chronicles, takes a pointedly didactic tone — the emphatic "he did very wickedly" carrying the implied thought that Jehoshaphat's alliance was therefore wrong, as the prophet had warned in 2 Chronicles 19:2.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley weighs the sin and its roots. It is mentioned, he says, "as an aggravation of his sin, after so great an obligation laid upon him by God, and after he had been so singularly reproved by a prophet, yet he relapsed into the same sin" — a fault that sprang partly from the near relation contracted between the two families, partly from the easiness of Jehoshaphat's temper, which could not resist the solicitations of others in things that seemed indifferent. He did not join Ahaziah in war, as he had joined Ahab, "but in a peaceable way only, in a matter of trade and commerce; and yet God reproves and punisheth him for it, to shew his great dislike of all familiar conversation of his servants and people with professed enemies of God." Ahaziah's "very wickedly," Wesley adds, means he wrought wickedness "industriously, and maliciously, and constantly," wholly given to idolatry.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the old weakness behind the new fault: Jehoshaphat still retained a partiality for the house of Ahab, having married his son to a daughter of that family, and now joined himself with Ahab's son not in war but in trade. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the timing and the rebuke it defied, Wesley the temper that yielded and the wickedness it embraced, Henry the family entanglement at its root. Together they show a good king's besetting flaw surviving even his greatest deliverance — that a man may be right in the main, and yet, by an easy fondness for ungodly company, sin against the very grace that has just saved him.
36:
The nature of the ill-starred partnership is now told — a joint fleet built for the sea. The reformed John Gill notes that Jehoshaphat "joined himself with him to make ships to go to Tarshish," and reconciles the notice with the parallel: though 1 Kings 22:49 reports that Jehoshaphat afterward refused to let Ahaziah's servants sail with his, that refusal came later, after he had been reproved and after the ships were wrecked. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds only the Targum's gloss on the destination, that "to go to Tarshish" means "in the great sea," by which the Targumists always meant the Mediterranean.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott handles the geography and the wording with his usual care. The parallel in 1 Kings 22:48-49 says Jehoshaphat made "ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold," but the vessels went not, being wrecked at Ezion-geber; and there is no mention there of a previous alliance with Ahaziah in the ship-building. The expression of the Chronicler's text, "ships to go to Tarshish," Ellicott judges an erroneous paraphrase of "ships of Tarshish" — that is, vessels built for long sea-voyages, "Tarshish-men," as we might say. According to Kings the ships were built to renew Solomon's traffic for gold from the Red Sea port; and Ezion-geber, where they were made and wrecked, was the Edomite harbour at the head of the Gulf of Akaba. If Tarshish means the Phoenician Tartessus in Spain, Ellicott observes, a fleet from that gulf could only reach it by doubling the Cape or crossing the Isthmus, so that some have supposed another Tarshish in the Persian Gulf or on the coast of India, a question he ties to his note at 2 Chronicles 9:21.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sums the venture: after God had given him not only victory but wealth, Jehoshaphat became partner with Ahaziah in a fleet bound for Ophir — a confederacy in commerce with a wicked king that was very ungrateful, whatever profit it promised. The witnesses do not divide. Gill harmonizes the trade with the later refusal, Clarke fixes the sea meant, Ellicott corrects the phrase and settles the port and the puzzle of Tarshish, Henry weighs the ingratitude of the whole design. Together they show the concrete shape of Jehoshaphat's compromise: not a battlefield but a shipyard at Ezion-geber, where a faithful king yoked his fortunes to an idolater's, and where, as the next verse will declare, the God who had lately fought for him would break the venture in the harbour before ever it put to sea.
37:
The chapter — and the reign's record — closes on a prophet's rebuke and a wreck in the harbour. The reformed John Gill identifies the messenger simply: Eliezer the son of Dodavah, of Mareshah, a city in the tribe of Judah. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that this Eliezer is otherwise unknown, his father's name properly Dodavahu, his town the Mareshah named in 2 Chronicles 11:8; and he sets the prophet's charge beside its precedent, for "because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah" answers exactly to Jehu the son of Hanani's earlier rebuke of Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab in 2 Chronicles 19:2. The word "the LORD hath broken thy works," Ellicott notes, is a prophetic perfect — He will certainly shatter them — and the shattering came, the ships "broken," that is, wrecked by a gale, as the psalmist sings, "with the east wind thou breakest the ships of Tarshish," in Psalms 48:7. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke records the Targum's rendering, "the Word of the LORD hath broken" the works — the same personal Word he had noted throughout the chapter.

Keil and Delitzsch read the sequence plainly: Eliezer prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying that because he had joined himself with Ahaziah the LORD had broken his works; and the ships were broken, so that they were not able to go to Tarshish. The venture never left the port.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the providence and the mercy together. God sent to Jehoshaphat, he says, to show him his error and bring him to repentance — both by a prophet, who foretold the blasting of his project, and by a storm, which broke the ships in the port before they set sail, so that the king was warned to break off his alliance; and it seems he took the warning, for when Ahaziah afterward pressed him to join again, he would not, as 1 Kings 22:49 relates. "See how pernicious a thing it is," Henry adds, "to join in friendship and society with evil-doers; it is a hard matter to break off from it." The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the unknown prophet and his charge, Clarke the Word that broke the works, Keil and Delitzsch the plain fulfilment, Henry the double warning of prophet and storm and the repentance it wrought. Together they end the chapter on a sober symmetry: the God who had shattered Jehoshaphat's enemies at the sound of praise now shatters Jehoshaphat's ships for the sake of his soul — the same hand, in judgment and in mercy, teaching a faithful but pliable king that the friendship of the ungodly is a yoke his God will not bless.
